Preference Relations and Axioms

This scene draws your preferences on the two-good plane.

A ranking is rational when nothing is left unranked. It also never loops back on itself. Such a ranking can be written as utility numbers, as in the formula below. Change the utility family and the whole curve map changes. You also see what breaks when an axiom fails.

For example, suppose a 🍎 apple bundle beats a 🍌 banana bundle. And the banana bundle beats a 🍞 bread bundle. Then the apple bundle must beat the bread bundle too.

x≿y  ⟺  u(x)≥u(y)x \succsim y \iff u(x) \ge u(y)x≿y⟺u(x)≥u(y)
complete+transitive⇒rational\text{complete} + \text{transitive} \Rightarrow \text{rational}complete+transitive⇒rational

Consider perfect-complements utility u(x1,x2)=min⁡{x1,x2}u(x_1, x_2) = \min\{x_1, x_2\}u(x1​,x2​)=min{x1​,x2​}.

Which of A=(4,4)A = (4, 4)A=(4,4) and B=(6,4)B = (6, 4)B=(6,4) is preferred?

Explain why the answer does not change even though BBB has more x1x_1x1​.

u(A)=min⁡{4,4}=4,u(B)=min⁡{6,4}=4u(A) = \min\{4, 4\} = 4, \qquad u(B) = \min\{6, 4\} = 4u(A)=min{4,4}=4,u(B)=min{6,4}=4
Show proof

  1. u(A)=min⁡{4,4}=4u(A) = \min\{4, 4\} = 4u(A)=min{4,4}=4 and u(B)=min⁡{6,4}=4u(B) = \min\{6, 4\} = 4u(B)=min{6,4}=4, so A∼BA \sim BA∼B — the consumer is indifferent.

  2. The indifference curve is L-shaped with its kink at (4,4)(4, 4)(4,4).

    B=(6,4)B = (6, 4)B=(6,4) lies exactly on the horizontal arm of that L — with x2x_2x2​ stuck at 4, raising x1x_1x1​ from 4 to 6 adds no utility at all.

    That is what "perfect complements" means: unmatched extra units of a good are worthless.
